title: Objects as Evidence
bigQuestion: How can a scorebook, a ticket or a ballpark plan be read as evidence, and who decides which objects are kept?

story.title: Two Papers in One Box
story.kicker: An archivist opens a gray box and sets two very different papers side by side.
paragraphs: In a quiet reading room, an archivist lifts the lid of a gray cardboard box. The box is acid-free, which means it will not yellow the papers inside. She wears no gloves, because clean, dry hands are safer for old paper than cotton gloves. A student sits across the table with a pencil. Pens are not allowed near the papers.

The first object is a scorebook from a baseball season in the early 1900s. Its pages are ruled into small boxes. A scorer has filled each box with letters, numbers and small marks in faded ink. On the inside cover, someone has written a name and a city.

The second object is a large folded sheet of heavy paper: a ballpark plan. It shows the outline of the stands, the diamond and the fences. Numbers along the edges give distances in feet. In the lower corner, a small box names the architect's office and gives a date.

The archivist points to a card tucked into the box. It carries a catalog number, a short description and a line about where the objects came from. A family gave them to the collection decades ago. That line, she explains, is part of the evidence too.

The student looks from one paper to the other. One was made in the stands by a fan or a club scorer, one pencil mark at a time. The other was made in an office before a single seat was built. Both are records of the same game, seen from two very different places.
story.think: Why might the note about where an object came from matter as much as the object itself?

lessons.title: The Scorebook and the Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick helped turn baseball games into printed numbers, and scorebooks became records historians can read.
reading: Henry Chadwick was born in England in 1824 and moved to the United States as a boy. He grew up with cricket, which already kept detailed written scores. In the 1850s he began writing about baseball for New York newspapers. He wanted readers to see a whole game in a small space.

Around 1859, Chadwick published a *box score*: a small table listing each player and what he did in the game. He adapted it from cricket scoring. He is often credited with using the letter K to stand for a strikeout. In 1860 he edited *Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player*, one of the first yearly baseball guides.

Newspapers printed box scores every day of the season. Clubs and fans kept their own scorebooks, bound books with a page for each game. These books recorded who played, in what order and what happened. They also often recorded the date, the weather, the ballpark and the crowd.

For a historian, a scorebook is a *primary record* of a single game. It can confirm a newspaper report or show where the paper got a fact wrong. The Baseball Hall of Fame elected Chadwick in 1938. He is still the only sportswriter enshrined there as a member rather than through a writers' award.

words.d: a small printed table that sums up each player's part in one game
a bound book in which a scorer records each game as it is played
an original account made at the time an event happened
an early yearly baseball guide, first edited by Henry Chadwick in 1860

check.why: Chadwick grew up with cricket and adapted its detailed scoring to baseball.

check.why: Chadwick was elected in 1938 and remains the only sportswriter enshrined as a member.

lessons.title: Tickets and the Gate
lessons.mainIdea: Tickets show who paid to see a game, what it cost and, in segregated places, where each person was allowed to sit.
reading: Early baseball was played on open fields where anyone could watch for free. In 1862, William Cammeyer opened the Union Grounds in Brooklyn, New York. He built a fence around the field and charged admission. It is often called the first enclosed ballpark. The fence made the game a business, because the *gate* could now be counted.

A *ticket* is small, but it holds many facts. It usually shows a date, a price, a section and a seat. It may name the club, the league and the printer. Saved tickets let historians compare prices across years and see which seats cost the most. Paper tickets were often torn at the gate, so a saved stub is usually the fan's half.

Tickets and seating charts also record *segregation*. In many ballparks, Black fans were kept to certain sections. At Sportsman's Park in St. Louis, Black fans were limited to the pavilion and bleachers until 1944. A ticket stub from such a section is evidence of a rule that kept people apart.

Tickets can also show who paid for a stadium and who profited. A stub may carry a tax line or a charity line. Collected together, stubs from one team over many years show how the gate grew and who could afford it. Many clubs now sell digital tickets, so paper stubs from recent seasons are becoming rare.

words.d: the money a club takes in from people paying to enter a game
a printed pass that lets a person into an event; it often shows date, price and seat
keeping people apart by race, by law or by custom
a field with a fence around it, so that the owner can charge admission

look.prompt: What can this stub tell you about the fan who held it and about the ballpark's rules?

check.q: Who opened the Union Grounds in Brooklyn in 1862?
check.why: William Cammeyer fenced the Union Grounds and charged admission in 1862.

check.q: What does the gate mean in sports business?
choices: the money taken in from paying fans
the office where rules are kept
check.why: The gate is the money a club takes in from admission.

check.q: Until what year were Black fans limited to certain sections at Sportsman's Park in St. Louis?
check.why: Sportsman's Park limited Black fans to the pavilion and bleachers until 1944.

lessons.title: Guides and Official Reports
lessons.mainIdea: Yearly guides and official reports gather rules, results and records into one printed place that historians can cite.
reading: After 1876, Albert Spalding's sporting goods company printed a yearly baseball guide. Henry Chadwick edited Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide for many years, until his death in 1908. Each edition held the season's rules, standings and records. Spalding's company also printed guides for football, basketball and other sports.

A *guide* was part rule book and part advertisement. Its pages sold Spalding bats, balls and uniforms. That mix matters to a historian. It shows that the company printing the rules also sold the equipment the rules required. For decades, Spalding also made the official ball of the National League.

The Olympic Games have their own printed record. The organizing committee of each Games publishes an *official report*. It lists the events, the athletes, the results, the budget and the buildings. The reports go back to the first modern Games in Athens in 1896.

Many official reports have been scanned and put online. The LA84 Foundation in Los Angeles, created with money left over from the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, keeps a large sports library. A student can read a report from a Games held a century ago, word for word.

words.d: a yearly printed book holding a sport's rules, records and results
the printed record an Olympic organizing committee publishes about its Games
the group in a host city that plans and runs one Olympic Games
a Los Angeles sports foundation funded by the 1984 Olympic surplus that keeps a large sports library

look.title: An Official Report's Contents
look.text: The report of each Olympic Games names the organizing committee, lists every sport and event, gives results for every athlete, and describes the stadiums, the budget and the ceremonies.
look.cite: Official Reports of the Olympic Games, 1896 onward, LA84 Foundation Digital Library
look.prompt: Which part of an official report would help you study who was allowed to compete?

check.q: Who edited Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide for many years?
check.why: Henry Chadwick edited the Spalding guide until his death in 1908.

check.q: Why does a historian care that Spalding's guides included advertisements?
choices: The company printing the rules also sold the gear the rules required.
Ads were banned by the National League.
Ads show the scores of games.
check.why: The mix shows a link between the rule book and the equipment business.

check.q: What does an Olympic organizing committee publish after its Games?
choices: a rule book for every sport
check.why: Each organizing committee publishes an official report of its Games.

lessons.title: Thirteen Rules, Two Pages
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith's original typed rules became a famous object, sold at auction in 2010 and now shown in Kansas.
reading: The thirteen rules James Naismith wrote in December 1891 survive as two typed pages. They stayed with the Naismith family for more than a century. They are the oldest known copy of basketball's rules. As a *physical object*, they are different from the printed copy in The Triangle.

On 10 December 2010, the auction house Sotheby's sold the two pages in New York. The buyer was David Booth, a businessman who had studied at the University of Kansas. He paid about $4.3 million. Booth was born in Kansas and later founded an investment firm.

Booth gave the rules to the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Naismith had coached basketball there from 1898 to 1907 and taught at the school for nearly forty years. The pages are now displayed on the Kansas campus in Lawrence, where Naismith is also buried.

The story of these pages is a lesson in *provenance*, the record of who owned an object and when. Each owner, from Naismith to his family to the auction to the university, is part of the object's history. A museum label that names that chain helps visitors trust the object is real.

words.d: a real thing that can be held and examined, such as a typed page, a ball or a ticket
the record of who owned an object and when, from its maker to today
a public sale where buyers bid against each other and the highest bid wins
a gift given to a museum, school or library

look.title: The Path of Naismith's Rules

look.prompt: How many years did the typed pages stay in private hands before the auction?

check.q: What auction house sold Naismith's original rules in 2010?
check.why: Sotheby's sold the two typed pages in New York on 10 December 2010.

check.q: What is provenance?
choices: the record of who owned an object and when
the price paid at an auction
the place where a game was played
check.why: Provenance is the chain of ownership of an object from its maker to today.

check.q: Why did David Booth give the rules to the University of Kansas?
choices: Naismith had coached and taught there, and Booth had studied there.
check.why: Naismith coached at Kansas from 1898 to 1907, and Booth was a former Kansas student.

lessons.title: A Ballpark on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Architects' plans record how a venue was meant to be built, who it was built for and when it changed.
reading: Every ballpark and arena begins as a drawing. An *architectural plan* shows the outline of the building from above. An *elevation* shows it from the side. Plans carry dimensions, materials, seat counts and the architect's name and date. Older copies of plans were often blueprints, printed as white lines on blue paper.

In Chicago, one architect designed two of the city's most famous ballparks. Zachary Taylor Davis designed Comiskey Park for the White Sox, which opened on 1 July 1910. He also designed Weeghman Park, which opened on 23 April 1914 for the Chicago Whales of the Federal League. The Cubs moved there in 1916. It was renamed Wrigley Field in 1926.

Plans record changes as well as beginnings. Wrigley Field's ivy was planted along the outfield wall in 1937. Lights were added in 1988, and the first official night game there was played on 9 August 1988. Each change produced new drawings with new dates.

Stadium plans also show public choices. Soldier Field, on Chicago's lakefront, opened in 1924. It was built by the South Park Commission, a public body, with public money. Its plans are public records. That makes it easier to see who paid and who decided.

words.d: a drawing that shows a building from above, with sizes and layout
a drawing that shows one side of a building as if seen straight on
a document made or kept by a government body that the public may see
a place where games or events are held, such as a ballpark, stadium or arena

check.why: Zachary Taylor Davis designed Comiskey Park (1910) and Weeghman Park (1914).

check.q: What was Wrigley Field called when it opened in 1914?
check.why: It opened as Weeghman Park for the Federal League's Chicago Whales and became Wrigley Field in 1926.

check.q: Why are Soldier Field's plans a public record?
choices: They were printed in a baseball guide.

check.why: The South Park Commission, a public body, built Soldier Field, so its plans are public records.

lessons.title: Cooperstown, 1939
lessons.mainIdea: The National Baseball Hall of Fame opened in Cooperstown in 1939, a site chosen because of a legend.
reading: Cooperstown is a small village in central New York. The Mills Commission's 1907 report had named it as the birthplace of baseball. Stephen C. Clark, a wealthy Cooperstown resident, saw a chance to draw visitors. He backed a museum there. It was planned to open in 1939, one hundred years after the date in the legend.

Voting began before the building was finished. In 1936, baseball writers cast ballots for the first inductees. Five players were elected: Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth, Honus Wagner, Christy Mathewson and Walter Johnson. Cobb received the most votes. On 12 June 1939, the *National Baseball Hall of Fame* was dedicated in Cooperstown.

For decades, the Hall honored only players from the white major leagues. Jackie Robinson was elected in 1962. In 1971, a special committee chose Satchel Paige, the first player honored mainly for his Negro Leagues career. In 2006, a special election added seventeen Negro Leagues figures. One was Effa Manley, co-owner of the Newark Eagles and the first woman elected to the Hall.

A hall of fame is a *museum*, but it is also a set of choices. Every plaque records a vote by a named body in a named year. Reading the list of who was elected, and when, is a way to study who baseball chose to remember. The Hall's library in Cooperstown also keeps scorebooks, contracts and photographs for researchers.

words.d: a person voted into a hall of fame
the museum and hall in Cooperstown, New York, dedicated on 12 June 1939
a place that collects, keeps and shows objects for the public to study
a metal plate on a wall that honors a person with a short written record

check.q: Who was the first woman elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame?
check.why: Effa Manley, co-owner of the Newark Eagles, was elected in the special 2006 vote.

check.q: When was the Baseball Hall of Fame dedicated?
check.why: The Hall was dedicated in Cooperstown on 12 June 1939.

lessons.title: Springfield and Canton
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball and pro football built their halls of fame in the cities where each claims its beginning.
reading: Basketball's hall is in Springfield, Massachusetts, where Naismith wrote his rules in 1891. The *Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame* was founded in 1959. Its first building opened on the campus of Springfield College on 17 February 1968. The Hall moved to a larger building in 1985 and to its current home by the Connecticut River in 2002.

Unlike the baseball hall, the basketball hall honors players, coaches and referees from every level, men and women, and from around the world. In 1985, it inducted its first women. Among them was Senda Berenson Abbott, who brought basketball to Smith College in 1892.

Pro football's hall is in Canton, Ohio. On 17 September 1920, team owners met in Ralph Hay's car showroom in Canton. They formed the American Professional Football Association. In 1922 it took the name National Football League. The *Pro Football Hall of Fame* opened in Canton on 7 September 1963.

Each hall ties its sport to a place and a founding date. That choice shapes what visitors learn first. A historian asks what each hall's founding story includes and what it leaves out, such as the older games that came before the famous date. Canton won the Pro Football Hall partly because the league began there and partly because local people raised money to build it.

words.w: Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame
words.d: the basketball hall in Springfield, Massachusetts, founded in 1959 and first opened in 1968
the professional football hall in Canton, Ohio, opened on 7 September 1963
the league founded in Canton in 1920 that became the NFL in 1922
the account a group tells about its own beginning

look.title: Two Halls, Two Doors
look.text: Visitor one walks into the basketball hall in Springfield and sees plaques for college coaches, Olympic players and women's pioneers beside pro stars. Visitor two walks into the football hall in Canton and sees busts of players, coaches and owners from the professional league.
look.prompt: How do the two halls define their sport differently? What does each choice include or leave out?

check.q: Where did owners form the American Professional Football Association in 1920?
check.why: Owners met in Ralph Hay's car showroom in Canton on 17 September 1920.

check.q: Which woman, who brought basketball to Smith College, was among the basketball hall's first women inductees in 1985?
check.why: Senda Berenson Abbott introduced basketball at Smith College in 1892 and was inducted in 1985.

check.q: How does the basketball hall differ from the baseball hall in whom it honors?
choices: It honors people from every level, men and women, from around the world.
check.why: The Naismith Hall includes college, international, women's and professional basketball.

lessons.title: Museums for Those Left Out
lessons.mainIdea: Museums like the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum, founded in 1990, keep records the older halls long ignored.
reading: Many Negro Leagues records were never kept in one place. Box scores appeared in Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier. White daily papers often ignored the games. Teams traveled constantly, and few clubs saved their scorebooks.

In 1990, a group in Kansas City, Missouri, founded the *Negro Leagues Baseball Museum*. Buck O'Neil, a former first baseman and manager of the Kansas City Monarchs, became its best-known voice. The museum stands in the 18th and Vine district, near the Paseo YMCA where the Negro National League was founded in 1920.

Other institutions collect the wider story of sport. The International Olympic Committee has been based in Lausanne, Switzerland, since 1915. It opened the *Olympic Museum* there in June 1993. Its collection includes torches, medals, uniforms and papers from the Games.

An *archive* is different from a museum. A museum chooses objects to display. An archive keeps papers, photographs and records mainly for study. Many teams, colleges and governing bodies have archives. Some are open to researchers by appointment. Researchers usually register first and follow reading-room rules, such as using pencils only.

words.d: the museum founded in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1990 to keep and tell the history of Black baseball
the International Olympic Committee's museum in Lausanne, Switzerland, opened in 1993
a collection of papers, photographs and records kept mainly for study
newspapers owned and written by Black Americans, such as the Chicago Defender

check.q: How is an archive different from a museum?

check.why: Archives keep papers and records for study, while museums display chosen objects.

check.why: Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier printed the games.

lessons.title: What, Where, Who Made It
lessons.mainIdea: A good museum caption says what an object is, who made it, when and where, and how it reached the collection.
reading: Museums label each object with a short text called a *caption*. A good caption answers a few questions. What is it? Who made it? When and where was it made? How did it reach this collection? The answers let a visitor judge the object as evidence. Many museums also post a longer panel nearby to tell the wider story.

Museums also give each object an *accession number* when it enters the collection. The number links the object to a file. That file records the gift or purchase, the date and the donor. It may also record repairs, loans to other museums and research about the object.

Take Naismith's typed rules as an example. A caption might read: Original rules of basketball, typed pages, Springfield, Massachusetts, December 1891. Written by James Naismith. Kept by the Naismith family; sold at Sotheby's in 2010; given to the University of Kansas by David Booth.

A caption must stay close to the record. If the maker is unknown, the caption says so. If the date is a guess, it says about or circa. A caption that claims more than the records show turns an object back into a legend. When a legend is well known, the caption can name it and say that the records do not support it.

words.d: a short label that says what an object is, who made it, when and where, and how it was acquired
the number a museum gives an object when it enters the collection, linking it to its file
about; used before a date that is close but not certain, often written c.
a person or group that gives an object or money to a museum

choices: It links an object to its museum file.

check.why: A caption stays close to the record and says plainly when a fact is unknown.

lessons.title: A Ball and a Legend
lessons.mainIdea: The Doubleday baseball, found in 1934, shows how an object can be real while the story told about it is a legend.
reading: In 1934, a baseball was found in a trunk in a farmhouse in Fly Creek, a few miles from Cooperstown. The ball was old, small and stuffed with cloth. The trunk was said to have belonged to Abner Graves, whose letter had shaped the Mills Commission's report.

Stephen C. Clark bought the ball. It became known as the *Doubleday baseball* and was shown in Cooperstown. It helped Clark and others win support for a museum there. The object seemed to prove the legend. The ball went on display in Cooperstown and is still part of the Hall's collection.

The ball is real. It is a genuine nineteenth-century homemade ball. But nothing on it connects it to Doubleday, to 1839 or to the invention of anything. Historians call this a problem of *attribution*: deciding who made or used an object. An object can be authentic while the story attached to it is not.

Today historians treat the Doubleday story as a legend. Bat-and-ball games were played in England and America long before 1839. Writers mentioned a game called base-ball in England in the 1700s. A good caption for the ball says what it is and where it was found, and labels the legend as a legend.

words.d: an old homemade ball found near Cooperstown in 1934 and linked, without evidence, to Abner Doubleday
deciding who made or used an object, based on evidence
genuine; really from the time and place it seems to be from
an object made or used by people in the past

check.why: The ball is authentic, but the story attached to it is a legend.

lessons.title: When the Record Changes
lessons.mainIdea: In 2020 Major League Baseball recognized seven Negro Leagues as major leagues, and in 2024 it added their records to its official statistics.
reading: For decades, Major League Baseball's official records included only the white major leagues. On 16 December 2020, MLB announced a change. It would count seven Negro Leagues, from 1920 to 1948, as major leagues. The first of them was Rube Foster's Negro National League.

Adding the records took years of work. Researchers searched old Black newspapers for box scores. The Seamheads Negro Leagues Database had gathered many of them. A research committee led by John Thorn, MLB's official historian, reviewed the numbers. Some games had no surviving box score, so the records are *incomplete*.

On 29 May 2024, MLB added the Negro Leagues statistics to its official *database*. Josh Gibson, a catcher for the Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords, became the career leader in batting average at .372. His .466 average in 1943 became the highest for a single season.

This change shows that a record is not fixed. It depends on which papers survived and which bodies decide to count them. A caption, a chart or a record book written before 2024 may now be out of date. Good history always names the source and its year.

words.d: a league recognized as the top level of professional play; its records count in official statistics
missing some parts; many Negro Leagues games have no surviving box score
an organized collection of records, often kept on computers so it can be searched
a historian named by a league or body to oversee its records
